blocks.text: This statement, however, is just as incorrect as that of Aristotle (l. c. 6, 3, 1) that the formation begins at the pointed ends; rather, the young bird develops from the middle.

The two Arabic translators do render אנפה (Lev. 11, 19), which belongs to the forbidden birds, by ببغاء ببجة [babbaghāʾ babbaja]; this, however, is not yet a reason to assume that the Talmud also regards the parrot as absolutely forbidden, all the less so as it does not take אנפה to be the parrot, see §. 200.

The explanation of the epithets שבור and פירוז may, admittedly, be attempted in various ways. שבור is supposed to recall the friendliness of the Persian king Sapor, namely the first of this name, who reigned from 242 to 272 C.E. and who, although depicted as a cruel and bloodthirsty tyrant (see Iselin. Histor. geogr. Lexicon part 4, p. 249), was nevertheless friendly toward the Jews. פירוז, on the other hand, recalls either Pyrrhus (Buxdorf Lex. p. 1806), which was the name of some well-known wicked person, or the later Persian king Perofes (reigned 359 — 485); but this is incorrect for the very reason that Rab, who names the two kinds of birds in our passage, lived much earlier (he lived in the time of Sapor); see Rappoport: Kerem Chemed part 6, p. 252 ff. — Perhaps both epithets are geographical names; thus there was in the vicinity of Nehardea a district named פירוז שבור, cf. Asaria de Rossi: Meor Enajim cap. 24. This district may have consisted of two parts, פירוז and שבור, and in their union have borne the common name פירוז שבור. Now perhaps the two parts followed different ritual norms, and in פירוז it was forbidden to eat the parrot, which was permitted in שבור; for an analogy to this see §. 186 and §. 211. — Most probable, however, is our explanation given in the text: to take שבור and פירוז in an appellative sense, although, to be sure, animals were not infrequently named after people, see §. 248, note.
Some would translate לילית (from לילה) at Jes. 34, 14 as Noctua, owl, see Univers israélite 12th year p. 502.
In Midr. Jalk. Schim. part 2, fol. 114, d, בר גזין should probably be read for בר זגין.

The goshawk, Falco palumbarius, was serviceable for hawking (hunting) hares, pigeons, partridges, pheasants, and also herons and cranes. In Arabic it is called Basi (plural Busat), from which, as Hammer thinks, the English buzzard, Bussard, arose, and which perhaps means the German „Baizvogel" (hawking bird); in Pers. too the falcon is called باز [bāz] and بازه [bāza], and similarly in Syr.: ܒܙܐ [בזא], and so the explanation of the Aruch, taking בואי as the name of a bird, may well be acceptable.

Rashi (Deut. 32, 11) says of the eagle that, in order not to frighten its young, it announces its arrival by beating its wings; further, that when flying out with the young it carries them above itself on its wings.
The work appeared anonymously (Brünn 1797), but the initial letters of the heading of the introduction to the work yield the names: אליהו בן מאיר ווילנא.

Lasch, in his excellent book פקודי ה' (p. 167), discusses the clean and unclean birds; the former may not be birds of prey and must be directed by nature to a diet of plants. „Their distinguishing marks,“ he says, „are: 1, an elongated middle toe on the feet, for scratching out the grains, 2a crop, for gathering them, and 3a stomach with a hard lining for grinding them, from which the hard skin can easily be peeled off.“
Later writers, such as Salomon Algasi in his work אהבת עולם (Dyrhenf. 5453) p. 113b, read כורביא, which does indeed recall corvus.
In Reggio's edition of the Pentateuch האנפה stands here erroneously for האנקה.

Ps. 104, 17 says: the חסידה has its nest on firs or cypresses (ברושים); on this the Midrash (Rabba Schemot fol. 152, c) raises the question: Does the stork really nest on such trees (cedars, ארזים)? And it therefore would not have חסידה in that passage understood as the stork; it is, however, correct that this bird nests on trees in the East, where the houses are mostly low; cf. Rosenmüller (Alterth. 4, 2, p. 320).
In contrast to the eagle (Jalkut Schim. part 2, fol. 145b; and Jerusalem Talmud Kiduschin 61, c).
Others translate לוך by λοπός [lopos], onion skins.
This, however, applies only to the small Egyptian raven, cf. §. 211.

Of partridges Aristotle says (Thierg. 5, 4, 7): The female partridges are even impregnated when they stand facing the males against the wind; often also when in the rutting season they hear their voice, indeed even when the males fly over them and their breath blows upon them.
This difference too deserves attention in determining the authorship of that commentary; cf. §. 164.
„Grave bird“ is called בת קברייא (Buxdorf Lex. p. 1963), which makes it all the more improbable that the mascul. form קברין should also be the same.
According to Jalk. Schim. part 2, fol. 13, d, this is supposed to be the טוס, peacock.
Arabic وز [wazz] and إوز [iwazz], and so אווזא is probably more correct than אווזא.
Note here the distinction that Rashi makes, in explaining קועיה in the case of the goose as beak, and the same word in the same passage in the case of the camel as neck; see §. 243.

In this passage it reads משחא דגרפא דאווא; whereas in the parallel passage A. Sara 28a: משחא דאווא בגרפא דאווא, which Rashi explains: goose grease, or goose fat smeared on with a goose feather; in any case only the goose is meant here, and Landau errs when in the Marpe Laschon on the first passage he explains כנ"יל as Caille, quail; perhaps the foreign word is the French canne (Spanish cañilla), reed, here the reed-like hollow wing bone; it may also be related to canal.
